title: Packaging Is a Brand's Face, and It Tells a Story. What Will It Look Like in 2016?
excerpt: We follow a handful of trends to see how packaging design should weigh what customers need and expect, so that they are glad to take a brand's products home.
body:
The job of packaging design is simple: catch the eye of a potential buyer, then persuade them to pay for the product.

Four months ago we wrote [an article about good-looking product packaging](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/16769.html), which explored how brands use creative packaging to win over consumers. Packaging, we said, is a brand's face, and it tells a story.

Looks aside, packaging can help a product stand out from its competitors in another way: by convincing consumers that the product meets their needs and is exactly the one they want (or might need). Luxury packaging, for instance, tends to use high-quality materials and fine workmanship; fresh-food packaging may have a small clear window so you can see the food inside.

"As brands try to offer consumers more personalized experiences, consumers in turn expect packaging to meet similar needs," writes the British market research firm Mintel in its newly released [*Global Packaging Trends 2016* report](http://www.mintel.com/global-packaging-trends). In other words, as consumer needs grow more specific and more varied, packaging has to respond.

Drawing on what consumers want in areas such as environmental friendliness, personalization and mobile interaction, the report forecasts the consumer-goods packaging trends that will shape the industry in 2016. We follow these trends to see how packaging design will weigh customers' new needs and expectations, so that they are glad to take a brand's products home.

## Saying it simply and clearly

Plenty of people like "minimalist packaging." When we talk about such designs, we often say they strip away clutter and useless information, look refined and pure, and easily stand out and catch the eye.

That is true. But consumers now expect to know more about what they buy. Mintel's report finds that 58% of British consumers look at the ingredient information on packaging, and 76% check whether artificial preservatives are used. In response, packaging design will pay more and more attention to plain function. Consumers care more about a product's ingredients, safety and purpose, yet they do not want to wade through confusing text. How can a brand tell them what they need to know simply and clearly? Doing so gives consumers a clearer, more immediate sense of what is in the package, and it shortens the time they take to decide.

The fragrance brand CLEAN prints product information directly on the boxes of its CLEAN RESERVE line. CLEAN's stated philosophy is "to blend high-quality scents from pure, sustainable raw materials." Its white paper box has a wood-grain texture; the product's name, scent family, notes and the perfumer's inspiration are printed clearly in the center, and more detailed information is printed on the inside of the box.

The bottle follows the same approach. It has a cap of Spanish oak and a simple square body with rounded edges, and a linen label on the front also carries product information. The package as a whole conveys the brand's philosophy, and everything a buyer wants to know is clear at a glance.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125051B48ChVHdEcaGDUSW.jpg-w600)

![CLEAN RESERVE packaging. Image source: [davidhelddesign](http://www.davidhelddesigns.com/#!public/csac)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125052Y58Qx7VU4zFIP2gt.jpg-w600)

For products with complicated information, this is harder to pull off. But some designers have tried creative solutions, and in an industry that can seem serious and rigid. The industrial designer [Joey Cheng](http://www.joeycheng.com/tylenol-care/) designed medicine packaging for the drug brand Tylenol, so far only as a concept. The Care+ line, aimed at children, is shaped like a pill and comes apart into a container and a dosing cup. The front shows a cute cartoon, with large type reading "I have a fever," "I have a cough" or "I'm in pain," and small type explaining what the medicine does; the back carries more detailed drug information and directions for use. The design is simple, fun and practical, and it brings the product closer to the people who use it.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125052sjc4uMeQnVXodEJG.jpg-w600)

![Tylenol Care+ packaging (concept). Image source: [Joey Cheng](http://www.joeycheng.com/tylenol-care/)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125053P0t3ReubSpFc8NJO.jpg-w600)

## Softer

Flexible packaging is already part of everyday life: soft snack bags and flat-bottomed laundry-detergent pouches that stand upright both belong to this category. What you may not know is that flexible packaging has been one of the fastest-growing categories in the packaging industry over the past decade. According to [a report by Smithers Pira](http://www.smitherspira.com/products/market-reports/packaging/flexible-packaging/the-future-of-global-flexible-packaging-markets), a consultancy that specializes in packaging and printing, the global flexible packaging market is growing at an average of 3.4% a year, and sales will reach US$248 billion over 2015-2020.

There are many reasons for its popularity. Consumers like that it is light, easy to carry and well sealed, and that some kinds can be resealed after opening. For brands and manufacturers, the same qualities mean easier shipping and better preservation and protection of the product.

Manufacturers also note that it uses less material than a rigid box, which lowers material costs. Just as important, flexible packaging is easy to adapt to all kinds of shapes, sizes and forms, and adding zippers, caps or handles is not hard, so it can do more and suit many different products.

Food is the most typical use of flexible packaging. NOKA, a brand of blended fruit-and-vegetable purées, packs its products in soft stand-up pouches with a small cap, a bit like the "drinkable jelly" pouches sold in Chinese supermarkets. The design also fits the previous trend: it tells you simply and clearly which fruits and vegetables are in the blend, how much it weighs and what quality certifications it holds. The ingredients themselves appear as fruit and vegetable illustrations printed on the white pouch, vivid and appealing; look carelessly and you may not notice that the top and bottom halves show two different ingredients.

[NOKA's own explanation of why it uses this packaging](http://www.nokaorganics.com/pages/faq) is much the same as ours. In short, it keeps the product fresh and moist, and it is light and durable.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125053Dn9jvSztOXqy5mQr.jpg-w600)

![NOKA packaging. Image source: [NOKA](http://www.nokaorganics.com/)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607031250530INc1ljYHkVPWhpo.jpg-w600)

Because flexible packaging is used so widely and is growing so fast, brands need to do more than enjoy its advantages: they must also make sure they stand out, or they will be lost in the crowd.

## More sizes

Packaging design has one measure that is rarely discussed but matters enormously: size. No product designer or brand can ignore it, and it is becoming ever more important to a brand's product strategy.

Mintel's report lists some findings: households around the world increasingly see large containers of milk as better value than they once did; 39% of British consumers want more alcoholic drinks in small bottles; and 50% of health-conscious snack buyers say they are willing to try new products in small trial sizes. "This shows that as brands keep expanding their product lines, meeting consumers' needs at different times and on different occasions means offering more sizes: smaller small ones and larger large ones," the report concludes.

The demand for more sizes is also tied to how people live. Take young office workers in cities. They live alone or share a flat with one or two others, so smaller portions suit them better; they watch their weight, so a small pack of high-calorie food is enough. On top of that, [they have relatively tight budgets and pay closer attention to spending, so they compare sizes to find the better deal](http://www.thedieline.com/blog/2015/3/18/sizing-up-success-consumers-crave-packaging-size-variety).

Meat, sweets and drinks have all come in smaller packages in recent years, largely because people have grown more health-conscious and more concerned about their weight. Coca-Cola, Pepsi and Dr Pepper, which together hold 90% of the US carbonated soft drink market, have all launched small cans, and their competition has spread into small packs. [Since 2011, sales of Pepsi's 12-ounce cans, half-liter bottles and 2-liter bottles have fallen 2.6% every year, while its small packs have sold better each year, rising 1.8% annually](http://www.wsj.com/articles/smaller-sizes-add-pop-to-soda-sales-1453890601).

American soda drinkers now "want to drink a little less, but they still enjoy their favorite brands," Marty Ellen, Dr Pepper's chief financial officer, [told *The Wall Street Journal*](http://www.wsj.com/articles/smaller-sizes-add-pop-to-soda-sales-1453890601).

![Different sizes meet the needs of different groups of people. Image source: [thedieline](http://www.thedieline.com/blog/2015/3/18/sizing-up-success-consumers-crave-packaging-size-variety)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125054ynBxZatiEUHLMgle.jpg-w600)

![Mini cans helped lift Pepsi's sales. Image source: [ispot](http://www.ispot.tv/ad/7gL8/pepsi-mini-cans-mini-hollywood-featuring-cuba-gooding-jr)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125055fX76tIBrhJj0ScGk.jpg-w600)

## Green packaging is no longer just talk

What exactly are "green packaging" and "sustainable packaging"? Put simply, packaging, like a person, has a "life cycle" and affects the environment around it. We take raw materials from nature, design and process them into shape, use the package to hold a product, and once the product is used up we dispose of it: recycling, incineration, composting or landfill. Green packaging uses as little raw material as possible along the way, or does as little harm to nature as possible when it is thrown away.

Now that more and more people care about the environment, a brand that ignores it risks more than "looking irresponsible"; it may well lose customers. 63% of American consumers say that packaging that can be recycled or reused for something else is a main reason they buy a product. These consumers want to live greener lives, and a company whose products "help" them do so naturally wins them over. Mintel's report makes two suggestions: use alternative materials (palm fiber and reed fiber, for instance, can both replace conventional plastic in boxes), or use recyclable ones.

Big companies have started. In January this year McDonald's switched to new packaging and [announced that by 2020 all of its packaging will be made from 100% wood fiber](http://news.mcdonalds.com/Corporate/Feature-Stories-Articles/2016/Continuing-our-Journey-Toward-Sustainable-Packagin) (for napkins, cups, bags, boxes and tray liners), sourced from recycled material or certified forests. Tetra Pak, the well-known Swedish packaging company, announced earlier this month that it will bring its milk carton [Tetra Rex® Bio-based](http://www.tetrapak.com/cn/packaging/tetra-rex) to the US market. The carton uses a renewable bioplastic made entirely from sugarcane grown on degraded pastureland. It went into use in Europe in January last year but is only now arriving in the US, where [Tetra Pak plans to ship 100 million of them](http://www.tetrapak.com/about/newsarchive/more-than-100-million-fully-renewable-packages-2016).

![McDonald's new packaging. Image source: [Mcdonalds](http://news.mcdonalds.com/Corporate/news-stories/2016/A-New-Year-and-A-New-Look-for-McDonald-s-Global-Pa)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125055v6fMg7hL94yKYBea.jpg-w600)

Small companies are bolder still. In 2014, "This Too Shall Pass," a series of food packages by the Swedish design studio Tomorrow Machine, drew wide attention. The studio used naturally biodegradable materials (caramel coated in beeswax, and agar) to package olive oil, raspberry smoothie and basmati rice. The packages do no harm to the environment, and they look simple and bright.

[Anna Glansén, one of Tomorrow Machine's founders, told QDaily](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/2254.html) that the design was inspired by biomimicry. The team wanted nature itself to solve the environmental problem, which led them to think of fruit peels and eggshells.

![Products from left to right: basmati rice, olive oil, raspberry smoothie](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125056VJK7fcWUdQM86nEZ.jpg-w600)

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125056kuM5vDETHG7yA6SJ.jpg-w600)

![The package shrinks as time passes. Image source: Tomorrow Machine](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125057kvpRT1BcQZagFjUe.jpg-w600)

## Digital printing may reach a tipping point

"Foodie," "Goddess," "Hipster," "Real Man"... In 2013, Coca-Cola's series of "nickname bottles" stuck in many people's minds. That summer, the bottles, printed with popular internet slang, helped Coca-Cola's sales in China grow [20%](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/8422.html) over the same season the year before.

The bottles were part of a Coca-Cola marketing campaign called "Share a Coke." The campaign actually began in Australia in 2011, when Coca-Cola printed the 150 most common local names on its bottles to connect with more consumers. It was a great success, lifting sales in Australia by [7%](http://www.bnext.com.tw/column/view/id/34398), and when it reached the US in 2014 it brought [the first sales growth since 2000](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/8422.html).

Our point here is not packaging as a marketing tool but digital printing. This Coca-Cola line was printed digitally, and the success of Share a Coke put the digital printing behind it in the global spotlight.

The biggest difference between digital and traditional printing is that the latter uses printing plates, turning out hundreds of thousands or millions of copies from one template, while digital printing prints a digital image straight from a printer, with no need to keep changing plates. So if you print labels or packaging digitally, you need less time, you get to market faster, and you can customize products more easily (Coca-Cola's name bottles met consumers' appetite for personalization very well).

Coca-Cola also set up a dedicated website where consumers can design their own bottle online and choose what is printed on it. Image source: [Shareacoke](http://www.shareacoke.com/)

In February this year, [Coca-Cola in the US launched new packaging for Diet Coke](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/21769.html). The campaign, themed "It's Mine," was a partnership with HP: designers first created 36 basic patterns, then HP's printing software combined them at random, automatically generating several million unique bottle designs, which were then printed. [Other brands that have worked with HP on printed packaging include Budweiser and Oreo](http://www.packagingnews.co.uk/news/materials/corrugated/exclusive-hp-readies-for-further-digital-print-growth-in-2016-23-12-2015), all using digital printing for products personalized for individual buyers.

![Diet Coke packaging. Image source: [gafollowers](http://www.gafollowers.com/diet-coke-gets-new-colorful-packaging/)](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160703125057l4TJWHDjkfP7wyca.jpg-w600)

Mintel's report notes that digital printing already accounts for 10% of the global packaging decoration market and has grown faster than the industry expected. The report also predicts that digital printing will reach a tipping point in 2016, spreading from limited editions and personalized products to mainstream packaging.

## More ways to interact in a "mobile" world

The world is getting smarter, and so is packaging, perhaps a little smarter than you think. QR codes on packaging have long been old news; and before most people knew what near-field communication (NFC) or Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) were, both were already being built into product packaging. Brands have realized that their customers are absorbed in the mobile world, so they are trying to use mobile interaction technology to reach these people and start a conversation.

You are probably more familiar with near-field communication (NFC, a short-range wireless technology); Apple's recently launched Apple Pay uses it. With built-in NFC chips, two devices held close together can transfer data and exchange information without a network connection. Apple Pay works by holding a phone near a point-of-sale terminal fitted with an NFC module.

NFC is now used in quite a few product packages. You might not expect it, but liquor brands have moved fairly quickly. They have long struggled with counterfeits, and now they embed NFC chips in their packaging. Consumers install the matching app on an NFC-enabled mobile device and hold it near the package to see whether the bottle has been opened and whether the liquor is genuine. [Companies doing this include the Scotch whisky brand Johnnie Walker and France's Rémy Martin (which puts the chip in the cork)](https://econsultancy.com/blog/66690-nfc-technology-in-packaging-does-it-have-a-future/), and [the closure maker Guala Closures Group announced last month that it is working with the chipmaker NXP to produce NFC-enabled bottle caps](http://www.nfcworld.com/2016/01/19/341361/nxp-guala-add-nfc-security-wine-spirit-bottle-caps/).

The pharmaceutical industry has begun to try the technology too. [The Tylenol Care+ packaging we mentioned earlier is designed to include BLE and NFC](http://www.joeycheng.com/tylenol-care/), so consumers can use it to learn more about the medicine and get help taking it. And as of January this year, the medical packaging company Jones Packaging Inc. was already working with the electronics supplier Thin Film to develop [a similar smart-packaging system](http://www.nfcin.com.cn/news/201512/24104749.html).

New mobile interaction technologies could find many more uses in product packaging.
